newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Germany agonises over memorial to Jews.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germany agonises over memorial to Jews.

text.p: More than a half century after the liberation of Auschwitz, Germany is still searching for a way to honour the memory of six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
The plan is to erect a central monument in Berlin, the Memorial for the Murdered Jews of Europe, to commemorate Germany's shame and sorrow over the Nazi genocide.

It has been allocated a plot of land in the new federal government quarter, a 15 million mark ($10 million) budget and the groundbreaking ceremony is scheduled to take place on January 27, 1999, 54 years after the liberation of the Auschwitz death camp.
No one doubted the benefits of such a project at first.

But years of wrangling over how it should look have now plunged politicians, historians, artists and Holocaust survivors into soul-searching and some commentators are beginning to cast doubt on the project itself.

"A central memorial is the fundamentally wrong way to mark the Holocaust," commented the weekly Die Zeit. "The question of national guilt would not be raised but silenced as we shout to state guests and tourists "Look, we've learned our lesson!'"
In a last-ditch effort to reach a consensus the parties involved, who have been arguing for nearly a decade, came together this month in a series of forums in Berlin.

Participants hope to arrive at a unanimous decision on a design in April. They will then deliver it to the city, the federal government and a citizen's intiative -- the three parties who will approve the final plan in mid-1998.
WHAT A MEMORIAL SHOULD NOT BE
The parties have so far only been able to agree on what they do not want: a concrete slab the size of a football field with the names of 4.2 million of the murdered Jews etched upon it.
This was the initial memorial blueprint -- after it emerged as the jury's favourite in a 1995 design competition.

But that entry by artist Christine Jakob-Marks is now considered a distant contender for the final form after Chancellor Helmut Kohl and members of the Jewish community criticised it for its "gigantism".

Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen joined the chorus of critics, saying that he would fight to keep a massive-scale Holocaust memorial from turning the new German capital city into "the capital of remorse".

Several panellists at the Berlin forums held up the Vietnam Memorial in Washington and Israel's Yad Vashem memorial to Holocaust victims as projects which had succeeded in helping countries to heal their historical wounds.
Planners hope the memorial can serve as the appropriate legacy of the generation that accepted the need to honour the memory of those who died in the Holocaust.

"Future generations may see things in a different way," said Berlin Culture Senator (Minister) Peter Radunski at the Berlin forum. "But they should and will see how our generation tried to deal with the need to remember six million murdered European Jews."
THE SEARCH FOR CONSENSUS

The idea for such a memorial came from a circle of media figures, historians and individuals in 1988, led by popular television chat-show host Lea Rosh. The group eventually won the support of central government and Berlin local authorities.

Germany donated a 20,000 sq metre (215,000 sq foot) plot of prime real estate for the Jewish memorial near the federal government quarter now under construction, between the Brandenburg Gate and the unmarked spot where Adolf Hitler's bunker stood.
It was then that the discussion seemed to stall.

The Berlin series of forums brought together 70 historians, artists, politicians and community and religious leaders to address why it was necessary to have a memorial, how it should look and where it should stand.

Yet even before the start of the meetings, observers questioned whether the panellists could achieve their goal of coming to a unanimous recommendation for the design of the memorial, which is due after their final meeting in April.

"The colloquia will develop into a farce if its sponsors have their way," said Gerhard Schoenberner, former director of the Wannsee Conference Museum, the villa in southwestern Berlin where Hitler's lieutenants plotted the "Final Solution."
"I see the great danger that they will agree to pick the least of the evils or make a lazy compromise."

One bitter rift between Gypsies who asked to be included in the project because of their losses in the Holocaust and Jews has been resolved with the promise to grant Gypsies their own memorial. Gays are continuing a lobbying effort for recognition of their suffering under the Nazis.
To many commentators, the anguished debate that has arisen here appears reflective of the culture that is staging it.

"The whole thing is a very German debate," Rosh told the socialist daily Neues Deutschland. "Other countries, for example Belgium, didn't have these long discussions about the issues surrounding a Holocaust memorial. They just built it."
Other observers welcome the chance to talk about the painful history that no one believes has been put to rest.

"Some say the objections and the debate about a Holocaust memorial have come 50 years too late and it is therefore rushed and not constructive," Salomon Korn, a leader of the Frankfurt Jewish community, wrote in the Frankfurter Allgemeine daily.
"But as long as a memorial remains unbuilt, it sparks a conflict with issues that it is never too late to discuss."
